rounds.t: Heart anatomy, pericardium, and coronary supply

q.s: A 46-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatic mitral stenosis reports progressive difficulty swallowing solid food. Barium swallow shows extrinsic compression of the mid-esophagus. Enlargement of which cardiac chamber best explains this finding?
e: The RV is the most anterior chamber, lying behind the sternum, far from the esophagus.
The RA forms the right heart border and lies away from the esophagus; it is not the chamber that compresses it.
Correct. The LA is the most posterior part of the heart and sits directly in front of the esophagus; mitral stenosis enlarges it and can cause dysphagia.
The ascending aorta lies anteriorly and is not affected by mitral stenosis.
The LV forms the apex and much of the inferior surface; it does not typically compress the esophagus.

q.s: The same patient later develops a hoarse voice. Laryngoscopy shows left vocal cord paralysis. Compression of which structure by the enlarged chamber explains her hoarseness?
e: Correct. An enlarged LA can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (a vagal branch), causing hoarseness, known as Ortner syndrome.
Sympathetic chain compression causes Horner features, not hoarseness.
The superior laryngeal nerve arises high in the neck and is not near the heart.
The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm and pericardium; its compression does not cause hoarseness.
The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the right subclavian artery, away from the left atrium.

q.s: The eponym for hoarseness caused by cardiac chamber enlargement compressing a vagal branch is:
e: Beck triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) describes cardiac tamponade.
Horner syndrome results from interruption of sympathetic fibers to the face and eye.
Correct. Ortner syndrome is hoarseness from left recurrent laryngeal nerve compression, classically by an enlarged left atrium.
Eisenmenger syndrome is reversal of a left-to-right shunt due to pulmonary hypertension.
Kartagener syndrome is a ciliary dynein defect with dextrocardia and situs inversus.

q.s: A 22-year-old man is stabbed just left of the sternum at the 4th intercostal space. Which cardiac chamber is most likely to be injured?
e: The LA is the most posterior chamber, shielded by the rest of the heart.
The coronary sinus lies in the posterior AV groove, far from an anterior stab.
The RA forms the right border and is less exposed anteriorly than the RV.
The LV lies more left-lateral and posterior; it is injured less often than the RV in anterior trauma.
Correct. The RV is the most anterior part of the heart and is the chamber most commonly injured in trauma.

q.s: On a cardiac CT, the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of the heart is assessed. Approximately what proportion of this surface is formed by the left ventricle?
e: The split is unequal; the LV contributes more than half.
About one-third is formed by the RV, not the LV.
The LV is the major contributor to the diaphragmatic surface.
Correct. The LV forms about 2/3 and the RV about 1/3 of the inferior cardiac surface.
The RV also contributes to the diaphragmatic surface.

q.s: Which sequence correctly lists the layers of the pericardium from outermost to innermost?
e: The fibrous layer is the outermost; parietal serous pericardium lies inside it.
Correct. Outer to inner: fibrous pericardium, parietal pericardium, then epicardium (visceral pericardium).
This lists the layers from inside out.
The epicardium is the innermost pericardial layer, lying on the myocardium.
The fibrous pericardium cannot be the innermost layer.

q.s: During pericardiocentesis, the needle enters the space that normally contains a thin film of serous fluid. This pericardial space lies between which two layers?
e: These are layers of the heart wall itself, not the pericardium.
The epicardium adheres directly to the myocardium.
Correct. The pericardial space lies between the parietal pericardium and the epicardium (visceral pericardium).
This is outside the pericardial sac.
These two layers are fused; there is no potential space between them.

q.s: A 30-year-old man with viral pericarditis has sharp chest pain that radiates to his left shoulder. Which nerve carries the sensory fibers responsible for this referred pain?
e: Correct. The pericardium is innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), so pericarditis can refer pain to the neck, arms, or shoulders.
Splanchnic nerves carry visceral afferents from abdominal organs.
The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior and carries no pericardial sensation.
The vagus carries visceral afferents but does not explain shoulder-tip referral.
Intercostal nerves supply the chest wall, not the pericardium.

q.s: Which coronary artery is most commonly occluded in myocardial infarction?
e: Correct. The LAD is the most commonly occluded coronary artery.
The RCA is commonly involved but is second to the LAD.
The LCX is less frequently occluded than the LAD.
The PDA is a terminal branch and less often the primary site of occlusion.
The acute marginal artery supplies the RV and is rarely the culprit.

q.s: A 58-year-old man has an MI involving the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum and the anterior wall of the LV. Which papillary muscle is also supplied by the occluded vessel?
o: Septal papillary muscle of the RV
e: The two LV papillary muscles have different supplies.
Correct. The LAD supplies the anterior 2/3 of the septum, the anterior LV surface, and the anterolateral papillary muscle.
The posteromedial papillary muscle is supplied by the PDA.
This is not a territory listed for the LAD and is not what this question targets.
The LAD territory includes the anterolateral papillary muscle.

q.s: A 64-year-old woman has an inferior MI. Two days later she develops a new holosystolic murmur from papillary muscle rupture. Which papillary muscle is most likely affected, and which artery supplies it?
e: The acute marginal artery supplies the RV free wall.
Correct. The PDA supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle, so inferior (PDA territory) infarcts threaten it.
The LAD supplies the anterior septum and anterior LV, not the posteromedial muscle.
The RCA does not supply the anterolateral papillary muscle.
The anterolateral papillary muscle is in LAD territory, not affected by an inferior MI.

q.s: Which territory is supplied by the posterior descending artery (PDA)?
o: Posterior 1/3 of the interventricular septum and posterior 2/3 of the ventricular walls
e: This is LAD territory.
Correct. The PDA supplies the posterior 1/3 of the septum, posterior 2/3 of the ventricular walls, and the posteromedial papillary muscle.
This is LAD territory.
The PDA does not supply the atria in this way.
The RV free wall is mainly supplied by the acute marginal artery.

q.s: A 70-year-old man with an acute inferior MI becomes bradycardic with complete heart block. Involvement of which artery best explains the conduction abnormality in a right-dominant heart?
o: Right coronary artery via the PDA
e: The obtuse marginal supplies the lateral LV wall.
Correct. In right-dominant hearts the PDA arises from the RCA and supplies the SA and AV nodes; infarction can cause bradycardia or heart block.
In a right-dominant heart the LCX does not give rise to the PDA.
Left main occlusion causes extensive anterior/lateral infarction, not isolated nodal ischemia.
The LAD supplies the anterior septum and LV, not the nodes in this pattern.

q.s: Coronary dominance is defined by the origin of which vessel?
e: The obtuse marginal arises from the LCX in all patterns.
The acute marginal arises from the RCA regardless of dominance.
The LAD always arises from the left main coronary artery.
The coronary sinus is a vein and does not define dominance.
Correct. Dominance is determined by which vessel gives rise to the PDA.

q.s: Coronary angiography shows the posterior descending artery arising from the left circumflex artery. This patient's circulation is best described as:
e: Correct. Left-dominant circulation means the PDA arises from the LCX; it is seen in about 5%–10% of patients.
The LAD does not give rise to the PDA.
Left dominance is a normal anatomic variant.
Right dominance means the PDA arises from the RCA.
Codominance means the PDA arises from both the LCX and RCA.

q.s: Which coronary dominance pattern is most common in the general population?
e: This is not a recognized dominance pattern.
Left dominance occurs in only about 5%–10% of patients.
Codominance occurs in about 10%–20% of patients.
Correct. Right-dominant circulation, where the PDA arises from the RCA, is the most common pattern.
Right dominance clearly predominates.

q.s: Blood flow through the coronary arteries supplying the left ventricle and interventricular septum is greatest during which phase of the cardiac cycle?
e: This is still systole, when LV coronary flow is reduced.
Flow is still diastolic but peaks earlier, in early diastole.
During contraction the myocardium compresses intramural vessels, reducing flow.
Systolic compression limits LV coronary flow during ejection.
Correct. Coronary blood flow to the LV and septum peaks in early diastole, when the myocardium relaxes.

q.s: A cardiologist cannulates the main venous drainage of the myocardium. Where does this vessel run and where does it empty?
o: Right AV groove; into the left atrium
Posterior interventricular groove; into the IVC
Left AV groove; into the right atrium
Anterior interventricular groove; into the SVC
Left AV groove; into the left atrium
e: The coronary sinus runs in the left AV groove and drains into the RA.
The coronary sinus empties directly into the RA.
Correct. The coronary sinus runs in the left atrioventricular groove and drains into the RA.
The anterior interventricular groove holds the LAD and great cardiac vein, which drains into the coronary sinus.
Myocardial venous blood returns to the right heart, not the LA.

q.s: A 55-year-old man has an isolated infarct of the right ventricular free wall. Which artery most directly supplies this region?
e: The LCX supplies the lateral and posterior LV.
The obtuse marginal (from LCX) supplies the lateral LV wall.
The LAD supplies the anterior septum and anterior LV.
Correct. The right (acute) marginal artery, a branch of the RCA, supplies the RV.
Diagonal branches supply the anterolateral LV.

q.s: On a posteroanterior chest radiograph, which structure forms most of the right heart border?
e: The RV is anterior and forms most of the anterior/inferior surface, not the right border on PA film.
The LV forms the left heart border and apex.
The LA is posterior; when enlarged it may create a double density but does not normally form the right border.
Correct. The RA forms the right heart border on a frontal radiograph, with the SVC above it.
The pulmonary artery contributes to the left upper heart border.
